nameStory: The 'mauve stinger' gets its name from its beautiful purple-pink coloration and its powerful sting that can leave you remembering the encounter for hours or even days. Its scientific name Pelagia noctiluca literally means 'she of the sea who glows at night' — a perfect description of this bioluminescent beauty that lights up the dark ocean waters.
description: The mauve stinger is a small but mighty jellyfish with a translucent bell that glows with stunning purple, pink, or mauve colors. Unlike most jellies, both its bell and trailing tentacles are completely covered in stinging cells, making it one continuous stinging machine. This oceanic wanderer is relatively small compared to other jellies, but what it lacks in size it makes up for in its brilliant bioluminescence and memorable sting. It's typically found in warm ocean waters but occasionally shows up in New England waters.

idTips.label: Purple-pink coloration
idTips.description: The bell has a distinctive mauve, purple, or pinkish hue that's visible even when translucent — no other common New England jelly has this rich purple coloring

idTips.label: Bell covered in stinging cells
idTips.description: The entire bell surface feels sticky or tacky to the touch (don't actually touch!) — most other jellies only have stinging cells on their tentacles

idTips.label: Bioluminescent glow
idTips.description: In dark water or when disturbed, the entire body produces an eerie blue-green light that pulses and flickers like an underwater lantern

idTips.label: Long trailing tentacles
idTips.description: Four long, thin tentacles stream behind the bell like purple ribbons, often extending much longer than the bell width

idTips.label: Small bell size
idTips.description: The bell is relatively compact and dome-shaped, smaller than a moon jelly but with a more pronounced dome

habitat: In New England waters, mauve stingers are occasional offshore visitors, typically found in deeper ocean waters beyond the continental shelf. They're most likely to be encountered during warm water intrusions from the Gulf Stream or after storms that push oceanic species closer to shore. When they do appear, they're usually found floating in open water rather than near the bottom or in shallow coastal areas.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen, but warm water events might bring them northward from more tropical waters as ocean currents shift.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for sightings when warm Gulf Stream waters occasionally push northward, bringing these oceanic jellies into New England waters.
seasonality.fall: Possible sightings continue as warm water masses linger, but populations typically move back to warmer southern waters.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in New England waters as they retreat to warmer tropical and subtropical regions.

funFact: This jellyfish has earned the nickname 'purple people eater' because its sting is so memorable that people can feel the burning, itching sensation for days or even weeks after an encounter — and the pain can be so intense that entire beaches get closed when swarms wash ashore!
confusionNotes: The purple coloration makes mauve stingers pretty unmistakable — most New England jellies are clear, white, or brownish. If you see purple in the water, it's almost certainly a mauve stinger. Remember: purple = powerful sting, so keep your distance!
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the beautiful 'mauve' name fool you into thinking this is a gentle species — this is one of the most painful stinging jellies you can encounter. The name 'purple people eater' isn't just playful; it reflects the serious impact these jellies can have on beach tourism and fishing industries when they appear in large numbers.
compareHints: The mauve stinger is the only species in its genus Pelagia, making it unique among jellies. Compared to other stinging jellies in New England like sea nettles, the mauve stinger's purple coloration and completely stinging bell surface set it apart. While sea nettles have long ribbon-like oral arms and are typically brownish or clear, mauve stingers are distinctly purple with simpler anatomy but more extensive stinging coverage.
